traveler: Claude des Armoises (Jeanne des Armoises, la fausse Pucelle)
title: The Grange-aux-Hormes to the Remission of King René: the Woman Who Came Back as the Maid
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Rome, penance for a blow struck at her mother
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed. Her Paris confession of 1440 gives no year; the only firm limit is that the episode precedes her appearance near Metz in May 1436. The year 1435, common in popular retellings, is unsupported by any source consulted, and one summary places the whole Roman episode before 1434.
stops.campa: Before she is anyone at all, by her own account, she strikes her mother. The blow carries her south over the Alps as a penitent, because absolution for laying hands on a parent belongs to the papal penitentiary and not to a village priest. Nothing else of her earlier life survives: no birthplace, no baptismal name, no family, no year of birth. The record of her existence begins in 1440, in a confession she is made to speak aloud at Paris, four years after she was already famous.
suggested_refs: The Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, the only source for anything in her life before 1436
sources: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, entry on the affair, 1440

stops.name: Rome, in the companies of Eugenius IV
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the same confession, which supplies no year. Sequence only: after the penance, before Metz in May 1436.
stops.campa: In Rome she puts on men's clothes and takes the pay of Pope Eugenius IV, who is at war in Italy with his own condottieri and short of soldiers. She serves in the papal companies through that fighting, and she kills two men. She says this herself, in Paris in 1440, when the pretence is finished and there is nothing left to gain by claiming it. Whether the campaign taught her to sit a horse and handle a sword, or whether she could already do both and that is why she was taken on, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Italian wars of Eugenius IV, in which she claimed to have served in male dress

stops.name: Grange-aux-Hormes, near Metz: the woman who calls herself Claude
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the Metz chronicle
stops.campa: Five years after the fire at Rouen, a woman is brought to a manor south of Metz to speak with certain lords of the city. The chronicle of the dean of Saint-Thiebault records the arrival in one flat line and gives her two names in the same breath: the Maid Joan who had been in France, and Claude, which is what she calls herself. This is Lorraine, the country Joan of Arc was born in, and no one at this table has seen Joan since Compiegne six years ago. The lords ride out to look at her.
stops.quote: Icelle année, le xx.e jour de may, vint la Pucelle Jehanne qui avoit esté en France, à la Grange-aux-Hormes, près de Saint-Privay; et y fut amoinnee pour parler à aucuns des seigneurs de Metz; et se faisoit appeller Claude.
stops.quote_source: Chronique du doyen de Saint-Thiébault de Metz, in Quicherat, Procès de condamnation et de réhabilitation de Jeanne d'Arc, t. V, p. 321
suggested_refs: Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 321-323, 'Documents sur la fausse Jeanne d'Arc qui parut de 1436 à 1440'
sources: Chronique de Metz, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 321

stops.name: Metz, recognized by tokens
stops.date_confidence: attested; the chronicle places the Messin recognitions on the day after the Grange
stops.campa: The next day the patricians of Metz come to her. She takes sire Nicole Lowe aside and says something to him in private, and the chronicle does not report what it was. What it reports is the effect: she was recognized by several tokens for the Maid Joan of France, the one who brought the king to be anointed at Reims. They give her a horse, weapons, a hooded cloak. A second manuscript redaction of the same chronicle, printed alongside the first, calls the whole apparition a supercherie.
stops.quote: et fut recongneu par plusieurs enseignes pour la Pucelle Jehanne de France, qui amoinnat sacrer le roy Charles à Reims
stops.quote_source: Chronique du doyen de Saint-Thiébault de Metz, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 322
suggested_refs: The second manuscript redaction of the Metz chronicle, Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 323, which calls the 1436 apparition an outright supercherie
sources: Chronique de Metz, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 322-323

stops.name: Metz, the brothers du Lys accept her
stops.date_confidence: inferred. The chronicle sets the brothers' visit within days of her appearance but gives no date.
stops.campa: Messire Pierre du Lys, knight, and the squire called petit Jehan du Lys come to see the woman at Metz. They are the brothers of Joan of Arc; they rode with her from Vaucouleurs to Reims and they buried nothing at Rouen, because there was nothing to bury. They look at her and they call her their sister. Nobody in the surviving record ever asks them why, and neither of them is ever recorded taking it back. Pierre will still be writing of Jehanne la Pucelle, sa soeur, seven years later.
suggested_refs: Donation of the Île-aux-Boeufs to Pierre du Lys, 28 July 1443, Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 212-213, in which the duke's own clerk writes 'en compaignie de Jehanne la Pucelle, sa soeur; avecque la quelle, jusques à son absentement, et depuis jusques à présent, il a exposé son corps et ses biens audit service'

A ducal treasury cédule of the same year 1443 paying ten livres tournois to 'messire Pierre Dulis, chevalier, frère de feue Jehanne la Pucelle', Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 214 n. 1, which flatly contradicts the reading of the donation
sources: Chronique de Metz, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 321-322

stops.name: Marieulles, three weeks with a noble house
stops.date_confidence: summer 1436. No source gives a month or a day; the interval of about three weeks is what the local accounts preserve.
stops.campa: She lodges some three weeks in the village of Marieulles, on the road between Metz and Pont-a-Mousson, with a noble family of the Messin country. Word travels faster than she does. People come to the house to see her and to test her, and the testing consists of asking a woman in men's clothes about things that happened at Orleans and Reims seven years earlier. She answers well enough that the visitors go home and repeat it. The house is not named in any source consulted.
suggested_refs: Marieulles, Moselle, 48.998 N / 6.101 E; several published summaries misplace it by three to five kilometres and one confuses it with Marville

stops.name: Liesse-Notre-Dame, the Black Madonna
stops.date_confidence: 1436; no month attested. The visit is reported as a waypoint on the road north to Arlon.
stops.campa: She turns north out of Lorraine to the shrine of the Black Madonna at Liesse, a pilgrimage the crowned heads of France have kept for two centuries and one that the real Maid never made. A woman claiming to be Joan going openly to a royal shrine is not hiding; she is being seen. The statue in the crypt is said to have been carried back from Egypt by three crusading knights of Eppes, and people come to it for cures and for the discharge of vows. The chronicle itinerary sets her at Liesse between Metz and the Duchy of Luxembourg, and says nothing about what she did there.
suggested_refs: The Basilique Notre-Dame de Liesse, Aisne, 49.6103 N / 3.805 E
sources: thehundredyearswar.co.uk, summarizing the Metz chronicle itinerary

stops.name: Arlon, at the house of Elizabeth of Görlitz
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged and not resolved. A registration at Cologne on 6 August 1436 requires her to have reached Arlon before that date, while other summaries place her arrival at Arlon in October 1436.
stops.campa: Elizabeth of Görlitz, dowager Duchess of Luxembourg, receives her at Arlon and keeps her. The duchess supported the Maid once and has money, a household, and a grievance against the Burgundians; whatever she believes, she gives the woman a roof for months. At Arlon she meets Robert, Count of Virneburg, who takes up her cause and will take her into the Rhineland. Gifts accumulate around her that summer, all of them from people who had been on Joan's side: a horse, jewels, a sword, a hooded cloak.
suggested_refs: Elizabeth of Görlitz, dowager Duchess of Luxembourg, and the network of former partisans of the Maid in Lorraine and Luxembourg

stops.name: Cologne, entered on the register as the Pucelle de France
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the Cologne record as relayed by montjoye.net
stops.campa: Virneburg brings her to Cologne, and in Cologne she is written down. The register takes the name she is using, Pucelle de France, and the city gives her a cuirass. Cologne is an imperial city with a cathedral chapter, a merchant council and an inquisitor, and none of them is a party to the quarrels of the French crown. She is a long way now from a manor south of Metz where the trick, if it is a trick, could still have been walked back over a meal. A clerk has entered it in the book, a German count has staked his name on it, and the cuirass is already fitted to her.
suggested_refs: The Cologne register entry naming her 'Pucelle de France'
sources: Chronique de Metz, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 323

stops.name: Cologne, the inquisitor Kalteysen
stops.date_confidence: the year is unsettled: one reconstruction places the process in 1436, another in 1437-38. No month is given by any source consulted.
stops.campa: Heinrich Kalteysen, inquisitor at Cologne, cites her: men's clothing, bearing arms, and magic. He has watched her dance with men and eat and drink more than her sex permitted. The charge sheet is the one read at Rouen five years before, in a different language. Trier is in schism, and what he has heard her boast is a political act rather than a party trick: that she can make Ulrich von Manderscheid archbishop of Trier as she once made Charles king of France.
suggested_refs: The Trier schism of 1430-1436 and the candidacy of Ulrich von Manderscheid
sources: Johannes Nider, Formicarius, c.1436-38, relaying the report of the Cologne inquisitor Heinrich Kalteysen

stops.name: Cologne, excommunicate for contumacy
stops.date_confidence: inferred. The summons, the failure to appear, the sentence and the departure are all undated in the Formicarius.
stops.campa: She does not appear. The court excommunicates her for contumacy, which is the sentence for not turning up rather than for anything she is accused of doing, and she leaves Cologne under Virneburg's protection and safe conduct. Nider, who wrote this down in his Formicarius, was not there; he is passing on Kalteysen's report at one remove, and the popular version in which Virneburg falls in love with her and hands her a company of soldiers has no source in Nider or in the Metz chronicle at all.
suggested_refs: Johannes Nider, Formicarius, book V, on the woman at Cologne

stops.name: Orléans, letters arrive from Jehanne la Pucelle
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: jeudi, veille Saint-Lorens, in the town register
stops.campa: She is not in the city. Her letters are. On the eve of Saint Lawrence the treasurers of Orleans pay forty-eight sous parisis to a pursuivant named Fleur-de-lilz for having carried the town letters from Jehanne la Pucelle, and they enter it in the register in exactly those words, with no qualifier and no doubt. Orleans was relieved by the Maid seven years ago and has kept her anniversary obsequies ever since. The same register that pays this messenger has already written 'feue Jehanne la Pucelle' three times.
stops.quote: A Pierre Baratin et Jehan Hombacheller, pour bailler à Fleur-de-lilz... pour don à lui fait, pour ce qu'il avoit aportées lectres à la ville de par Jehanne la Pucelle; pour ce, 48 s. p.
stops.quote_source: Comptes de la ville d'Orléans, 9 August 1436, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 326
suggested_refs: The Orléans anniversary obsequies of 1433, 1436 and 1439, which name 'feue Jehanne la Pucelle' in the same registers, Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 274-275
sources: Comptes municipaux d'Orléans, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 326

stops.name: Orléans, her brother asks the town for money
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: mardi 21 August 1436 in the town register
stops.campa: Twelve days later Jehan du Lys walks into the town chamber himself and asks the procurators for a little money to get back to his sister. He tells them he has come from the king, that the king ordered him a hundred francs and that only twenty of them were paid. The register names him as the brother of the said Pucelle, sets down his request in his own words, and records no question put to him. The town votes twelve livres tournois and disburses nine livres twelve sous.
stops.quote: pour don a lui fait, la somme de 12 livres tournois, pour ce que ledit frère de ladicte Pucelle vint en la Chambre de la dicte ville requérir aux procureurs que ilz lui voulsissent aidier d'aucun poy d'argent pour s'en retourner par devers sa dicte seur
stops.quote_source: Comptes de la ville d'Orléans, 21 August 1436, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 326
suggested_refs: The reading 'poy d'argent', a little money, which several modern retellings garble into 'poids d'argent', a weight of silver
sources: Comptes municipaux d'Orléans, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 326

stops.name: Arlon, inspected by the herald of Orléans
stops.date_confidence: attested; the town pays for a mission of six weeks, so the herald's arrival at Arlon is not fixed to this date
stops.campa: Orleans pays a pursuivant for a mission of six weeks: go to Arlon, see the Maid, and carry letters on from there to the king at Loches. So the town does check. A herald in the town's coat rides four hundred kilometres into the Duchy of Luxembourg to stand in front of her and look at her face, and then rides to the Loire to tell Charles VII what he saw. The register records the payment and nothing else, and the town goes on writing to her. What did the herald say?
suggested_refs: The herald Coeur-de-Lis of Orléans, sent to Arlon to verify her before the town committed further honours

stops.name: Arlon, the marriage to Robert des Armoises
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged. One source gives 3 October 1436 for the wedding at Arlon; several others give 6 or 7 November 1436, but that is the date of the Haraucourt sale contract and not of the wedding. The Metz chronicle records the marriage with no month at all.
stops.campa: She comes back from Cologne to Arlon and marries Robert des Armoises, knight, of a Lorraine house, a widower born about 1388 and therefore some forty-eight years old. He is marrying the Maid of France, or he is marrying a woman he knows perfectly well is not the Maid of France and taking the name anyway. The chronicle of Metz sets down the fact and not the reason. From this day she has a legal identity that outlives the claim: Madame des Armoises.
stops.quote: Et puis s'en vint à ladicte Arelon; et là fut faict le mariage de messire Robert des Hermoises, chevalier, et de la dite Jehanne la Pucelle.
stops.quote_source: Chronique du doyen de Saint-Thiébault de Metz, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 323
suggested_refs: Robert des Armoises, seigneur de Tichemont, b. c.1388
sources: Chronique de Metz, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 323

stops.name: Metz country, the Haraucourt sale contract
stops.date_confidence: 6 or 7 November 1436; sources differ by one day. The place of sealing is not stated in the printed text.
stops.campa: Robert des Armoises and his wife sell the revenues of Haraucourt and seal the deed jointly. She is named in it as Jehanne du Lys, la Pucelle de France, dame de Tichemont, wife of the seller. This is the hardest evidence in the whole affair and it proves nothing about who she was, only what she was called in a document that transferred property and could be pleaded in a court. A notary wrote la Pucelle de France into a contract of sale and nobody voided it.
stops.quote: Jehanne du Lys, la Pucelle de France, ma femme
stops.quote_source: Acte de vente of the Haraucourt revenues, 7 November 1436, printed in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 328-329, from Dom Calmet, Preuves de l'Histoire de Lorraine, t. III, col. CCCV
suggested_refs: Dom Calmet, Preuves de l'Histoire ecclésiastique et civile de la Lorraine, t. III
sources: Dom Calmet, Preuves, t. III, col. CCCV

stops.name: Metz, the married years
stops.date_confidence: 1436-37. No document fixes when the household settled or where exactly in the Messin country it stood.
stops.campa: For something like three years she lives in the Metz region as a knight's wife and goes on writing to Orleans and to the court of France under the other name. Both things are true at once and neither cancels the other. She is a landholder's wife with a seal and a household, and she is the Maid, and the same neighbours who watched her arrive at the Grange-aux-Hormes in men's clothes now watch her keep a house. The tours through Lorraine and Champagne continue in the intervals.
suggested_refs: The des Armoises holdings in the Messin country and at Tichemont

stops.name: Château de Jaulny, the two sons
stops.date_confidence: the two sons are attested by her own confession of 1440, which gives neither dates nor a place. Jaulny as their birthplace is château tradition only and is not corroborated by any document consulted.
stops.campa: She bears Robert des Armoises two sons. She will say so herself in Paris, under compulsion, in the sentence that ends the whole affair: not a maid, married to a knight, mother of two boys. Local tradition puts the births at Jaulny, the family seat in the wooded hills between Metz and Toul, where two painted medallions still face each other over a fifteenth-century fireplace and are shown to visitors as her portrait and her husband's. They were found under plaster in 1871.
suggested_refs: The two painted medallions at the Château de Jaulny, uncovered under plaster on a fifteenth-century chimney in 1871; the historian Pierre-Gilles Girault holds there is a strong chance they were painted in 1871 itself
The mayor of Jaulny's account, given in 1871, that his great-great-grandfather had hidden the portraits in the keep before the Revolution on the orders of M. des Armoises

stops.name: Le Mans, the company that was hers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The events are undated in the remission, which places them about two years before June 1441; the identification of this Jehanne with the woman of Metz is called only 'not impossible' in the literature.
stops.campa: A royal letter of remission granted five years later, to a Gascon squire pardoned for pillage in Anjou and Poitou, contains one sentence that has been read ever since as her military career. Gilles de Rais, Marshal of France, tells the squire he means to march on Le Mans and wants him to take charge of the men of war that a woman calling herself the Maid then had. She is not documented at Le Mans. Le Mans is the objective. What the sentence does establish is that somebody handed her troops away.
stops.quote: qu'il vouloit aler au Mans et qu'il vouloit qu'il prinst la charge et gouvernement des gens de guerre que avoit lors une appelée Jehanne, qui se disoit Pucelle
stops.quote_source: Letter of remission for Jehan de Siquemville, Saint-Denis, June 1441, Trésor des chartes J. 176 pièce 84, printed in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 333
suggested_refs: The chancery formula 'une appelée Jehanne, qui se disoit Pucelle', which withholds the definite article the town of Orléans was granting her freely in the same years

stops.name: Orléans, wine on her arrival
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the town accounts
stops.campa: This time she comes in person. The town buys wine for her arrival and enters it under the name dame Jehanne des Armoises. Orleans has been paying her messengers for three years without seeing her; now the woman herself rides through the gate the English abandoned in 1429, into a city that celebrates its deliverance every eighth of May with a procession and a mass for the soul of the dead Maid. She is lodged in the town's hospitality and fed at the town's expense for a fortnight.
suggested_refs: The Orléans deliverance procession of 8 May, kept annually since 1430
sources: Comptes municipaux d'Orléans, 18 July 1439, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 331-332

stops.name: Orléans, the supper she leaves early
stops.date_confidence: the food and wine entries of 29 and 30 July are attested; the anecdote attached to them is not documented and rests on a single modern secondary account with no primary citation.
stops.campa: A story goes with the fortnight and cannot be sourced past a modern retelling, which supplies no primary citation. She has been in the city eleven days. At a supper held in her honour she leaves before the end, and the reason given is that a tailor who once cut clothes for the real Joan was expected at the table. There is no register entry for the tailor, no name, no deposition. What the accounts for the twenty-ninth and the thirtieth of July record is meat and wine.
suggested_refs: The Orléans accounts for 29 and 30 July 1439, which record food and wine and nothing else
sources: Comptes municipaux d'Orléans, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 331-332
Mental Floss, anecdotal, no primary citation found

stops.name: Orléans, two hundred and ten livres
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the sum was voted after deliberation of the town council and paid on 1 August 1439, at the farewell dinner. Some accounts wrongly give 29 July.
stops.campa: Some accounts put this on the twenty-ninth of July; the register puts it on the first of August. The council deliberates and votes her two hundred and ten livres parisis for the good she did the town at the siege of 1429. It is not a gift to a guest. It is a payment for a service rendered ten years earlier by a woman burned in 1431, made out to the woman sitting at the farewell dinner and entered in the ordinary column of the town's expenses. She leaves that same evening, in haste, before the honours are finished.
suggested_refs: The deliberation of the Orléans town council preceding the payment of 1 August 1439
sources: Comptes municipaux d'Orléans, 1 August 1439, in Quicherat, Procès, t. V, pp. 331-332

stops.name: Orléans, the last propine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the town accounts
stops.campa: She is back in Orleans five weeks later and the town pays a propine, an honorary gift, to mark the return. Five weeks before that it had settled a debt of ten years standing with her in cash. This is the last certain sight of her in the city that had paid for her letters and sent a herald across Europe to look at her face. No entry records a quarrel, a suspicion, a refusal at the gate. After the fourth of September 1439 the accounts stop mentioning her.
suggested_refs: The Orléans propine of 4 September 1439, the final entry naming her

stops.name: Tours, her letters carried to the king
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the accounts of Tours
stops.campa: Tours pays a messenger to carry letters she has written to the king and to the bailli, riding between Tours and Orleans. Three weeks after the last Orleans payment she is still writing to Charles VII and a second town is still paying for the postage. That she writes to the bailli as well is the correspondence of somebody with business in hand rather than of a suppliant. The entry is dated the twenty-seventh of September 1439, and no clerk in either town has yet been told to stop paying for her messengers.
suggested_refs: The municipal accounts of Tours, September 1439

stops.name: Orléans, the secret between two people
stops.date_confidence: place not established and pinned here provisionally. Pierre Sala gives no location; one reconstruction proposes Bourges or Orléans in the autumn of 1440. Sala collected the story from Guillaume Gouffier in 1480 and wrote it out about 1516, some eighty years after the events, and it is treated as legendary elaboration rather than record.
stops.campa: The story is late, and it is the one everyone tells. The king puts a courtier in his place among a crowd to see whether she can find him. She finds him, they say, by a soft leather boot he wears over an old wound. Then Charles VII greets her gently and invokes the one thing she cannot have: the secret that is between the two of them. She kneels and confesses everything. Pierre Sala wrote this down eighty years later from a chamberlain's account, and no contemporary document contains a word of it.
stops.quote: Pucelle m'amye, vous soyez la très bien revenue, ou nom de Dieu qui sçait le secret qui est entre vous et moy.
stops.quote_source: Charles VII, as reported by Guillaume Gouffier, seigneur de Boisy, to Pierre Sala, Hardiesses des grands rois et empereurs, in Quicherat, Procès, t. IV, p. 281
suggested_refs: Pierre Sala, Hardiesses des grands rois et empereurs, presented to François Ier in 1516, MS 191 Suppl. fr.

stops.name: Paris, the marble table of the Palais
stops.date_confidence: autumn 1440. One source gives August 1440; another dates the amende honorable to September or October and explicitly denies August. No day is recorded anywhere.
stops.campa: The University and the Parlement bring her to Paris and set her on the pierre de marbre in the great court of the Palais, where sentences are read and mysteries are played, and make her speak. She says she is not a maid, that she was married to a knight, that she had two sons by him. She adds the blow to her mother, the pilgrimage to Rome, the pope's soldiers, the two men she killed. This is the only account of her own life that she ever gives, and the bourgeois of Paris writes it down without surprise.
stops.quote: elle n'estoit pas pucelle, et qu'elle avoit esté mariée à un chevalier dont elle avait eu deux fils
stops.quote_source: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, on her amende honorable at the Palais, 1440
suggested_refs: The pierre de marbre of the great court of the Palais de la Cité, the customary place of public amende honorable
sources: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, §790, Tuetey ed., pp. 354-355

stops.name: Paris, and then she went away
stops.date_confidence: inferred. The Journal closes its entry with this sentence and attaches no date to it.
stops.campa: The bourgeois ends the entry in four clauses and no judgement. She was at Paris, she went back to the war, she was in garrison, and then she went away. There is no execution, no imprisonment, no penance beyond the marble stone. A woman who impersonated the most famous person in France for four years, took money from two towns and commanded soldiers, confesses in public and is allowed to walk out of the city and rejoin a garrison. The bourgeois names no penalty and moves on to the next thing.
stops.quote: Et quant elle fut à Paris, encore retourna en la guerre, et fut en garnison, et puis s'en alla.
stops.quote_source: Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, §790, Tuetey ed., pp. 354-355; reprinted Quicherat, Procès, t. V, p. 335
suggested_refs: The Journal d'un bourgeois de Paris, 1405-1449, the only narrative source for the unmasking

stops.name: Sermaize, at table with the Voulton kin
stops.date_confidence: 1449 by the deposition of Jehan le Montigueue, aged 70, taken in 1476; the curé of the same parish testified in the same inquest that she came twenty-four years earlier, which yields about 1452. The contradiction stands in the testimony itself.
stops.campa: Nine years after Paris a woman still calling herself Jeanne la Pucelle is eating at Sermaize with the Voultons, who are the family of Joan of Arc's mother, and with Jehan du Lys, who is Joan's brother. Two witnesses will describe these dinners to notaries a quarter of a century later. Whatever was said on the marble table in Paris did not reach this room, or reached it and was set aside. The kin who would know best are the ones pouring the wine. The depositions are taken at Vitry, before notaries, in November 1476.
suggested_refs: The inquest of 2-3 November 1476 before the notaries of Vitry into the descendants of the brother of Joan of Arc's mother, an inquiry twenty years later than and entirely separate from the 1455-56 trial of rehabilitation
sources: Deposition of Jehan le Montigueue, aged 70, inquest of November 1476

stops.name: Sermaize, the game against the curé
stops.date_confidence: about 1452. Simon Fauchard, curé of Sermaize, aged 53, testified in 1476 that she came twenty-four years before, and one summary states explicitly that he affirmed the year as 1452 and not 1449.
stops.campa: Simon Fauchard, priest of Sermaize in the Marne, plays tennis against her. He is fifty-three when he tells the notaries about it in 1476. He says she came dressed as a man, that she came often over several years, and that the visits were joyful. He does not say whether he believed her, and the notaries do not ask him. What he remembers exactly is the line she gave him when the game was over: he had now played, she said, against la Pucelle de France.
suggested_refs: Depositions of Perinet de Voulton, carpenter, aged 52; Simon Fauchard, curé, aged 53; Jehan le Montigueue, aged 70; and Jehan Guillaume, aged 76, Vitry, November 1476
The phonetic accident by which Sermaize chimes with des Armoises, a probable source of confusion in later retellings; no source consulted derives either name from the other
sources: Testimony of the curé of Sermaize, inquest of November 1476

stops.name: Saumur, three months in the prison of King René
stops.date_confidence: inferred. The remission of February 1457 says she had been held about three months, which places the arrest in the late autumn of 1456; no arrest record survives.
stops.campa: She is arrested in the Angevin lands after a dispute with the Dame de Saumoussay and held about three months in the prison of King René. She is going by Jeanne de Sermaises now, after the village of the tennis game, and she is married to a man called Jean Douillet. She is about forty-four years old and twenty years into the name. The charge is not sorcery and not heresy. The charge is that she called herself Jeanne la Pucelle for a long time and deceived people who had seen the real one at Orleans in 1429.
suggested_refs: The dispute with the Dame de Saumoussay, the occasion of her arrest

stops.name: Saumur, the remission of King René
stops.date_confidence: February 1457; the day is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: René of Anjou releases her on a conditional ticket good for five years, on terms: that she bear herself honestly in dress and in other matters, as a woman should do. The document describes her as about forty-five years old and at present wife of Jean Douillet. If forty-five is right she was born about 1412, which is also the year given for the birth of Joan of Arc, and there is no way to tell whether that is a coincidence, a clerk's assumption, or her own final piece of work.
stops.quote: elle s'estoit fait appeller par long temps Jehanne la Pucelle
stops.quote_source: Letter of remission of René d'Anjou, kingdom of Anjou, February 1457
suggested_refs: The condition of the remission: that she comport herself honestly in dress and in other matters, as a woman should do

stops.name: Anjou, the record closes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The remission of February 1457 is the last document naming her; nothing establishes where she went, how long she lived, or where she died.
stops.campa: She walks out of the prison at about forty-five, under a five-year good-behaviour bond, with a husband and no name of her own left. For twenty-one years she was in the accounts of two towns, the chronicle of a third, the register of an inquisition, a contract of sale, a royal chancery and a pope's army. The remission of February 1457 is the last document anywhere that names her. No burial entry, no widow's suit, no further remission, no denunciation.
suggested_refs: The gap after February 1457, for which no source consulted offers any document at all
sources: thehundredyearswar.co.uk, synthesizing the terms of the 1457 remission

stops.name: Pulligny-sur-Madon, the tomb that claims her
stops.date_confidence: the stop is dated to Robert des Armoises's burial in 1450. Her own burial here is not attested. The plaque quoted was affixed in 1690 by the des Armoises family, two hundred and forty years later, and vanished about 1900; its wording is ambiguous as to whether the 1449 death date belongs to her or to Robert, and a death in 1449 is flatly contradicted by the Sermaize and Saumur records of 1452 and 1457.
stops.campa: Robert des Armoises dies in 1450 at Jaulny and is buried in the parish church of Pulligny, south of Nancy. In 1690 his descendants set a plaque above the tomb naming his wife as haute et honoree dame Jehanne du Lis la Pucelle de France, dame de Tichemont, dead on the fourth of May 1449. The woman it names was alive in Anjou eight years after that date. Visitors could still read the plaque in the eighteen-hundreds. It was gone by about 1909, and the stone frame beside the choir is empty.
stops.quote: Ci-git haute et honoree dame Jehanne du Lis la Pucelle de France dame de Tichemont qui fut femme de noble homme Messire Robert des Hermoises chevalier seigneur dudit lieu qui trepassa l'an 1449 le 4e jour de may
stops.quote_source: Plaque affixed in 1690 by the des Armoises family in the parish church of Pulligny-sur-Madon, transcribed before its disappearance about 1900
suggested_refs: The empty stone frame in the right-hand chapel beside the choir at Pulligny-sur-Madon, all that survives of the 1690 plaque
